prop: Every observation in this memo was taken against the tetel worktree at commit 74d4622d, the tip of main after PR #30. The worktree carried one untracked file (scratchpad_backup_jps.ts) that no observation here reads, and no modified tracked file.

At the pinned commit, a verification that ends `timeout`, `unavailable` or `unparsable` reaches the author as one `status` value on one reply: the one whose cursor position holds its record, since delivery is one record per call. That reply carries no `detail` for it, because `block` inserts `detail` only for `unauthorized`. Its `guidance` is the same constant sent on every status, and that constant describes a finding the model raised ("the two look inconsistent to it"), not a check that did not run. Nothing in any later reply refers to that mint's verification again.

Decision: the reply that delivers a record carries that record's `detail` whenever the record has one. That is every non-`ok` record, plus an `ok` whose literal, refuter or gate leg did not complete, because those are exactly the records whose detail is kept. The exception is any text the model or provider returned: it stays in verify.log and is never sent to the author. At the pinned commit, four of the 20 detail sources embed such text — the 200-character reply beginnings in the check leg, the typed call and the literal check, and the label string in parse_assertions. The other sixteen are fixed strings, an HTTP status code, a ureq transport error, byte counts, budgets or configuration. Keeping reply text out is the rule the module already applies to a model-produced span that fails verification: a fabricated span sends the reader to check against text that does not exist.

why: Its sixteen-other-sources clause rested on grep lines that show only the first line of four multi-line format! calls; F11 captures their bodies.

prop: Decision: reply text is split off at its four sources, not cut out of the finished string later. Each of those sites records the explanation as `detail` and the embedded model or provider text as a separate log-only field on the record. `block` reads only `detail`, and verify-report prints the log-only field only under `--spans`. The split also repairs the report. It dedups details as whole strings and truncates each to 160 characters, so a detail carrying a per-reply excerpt was unique on every record and was printed mostly as excerpt. Once split, identical causes collapse to one line. Every other detail source is reply-free today, but nothing stops a future site from formatting reply text into `detail` itself. So the guarantee is per-site, pinned by the tests below, not structural.

Decision: under `timeout`, `unavailable` and `unparsable`, `guidance` is a second constant, not GUIDANCE. It says three things: the mint named by `for_mint` was not checked; an absent `findings` means nothing was compared, not that nothing was wrong; `detail` says why. It also states what the author can do today. A revision whose proposition and citations are unchanged starts no new verification, so repeating the same text does not retry it; only a changed text or changed citations does. Under `ok`, GUIDANCE stays as written, because it describes findings and `ok` is the only status that carries them. Under `queued`, `skipped`, `off`, `gated` and `unauthorized`, GUIDANCE also stays. It misdescribes those replies too, but none of them is a verification that was attempted and lost. This design leaves them alone and records that as a residual.

why: The remedy sentence covers fact and prose mints too; F4 is claim-only, F13 shows the same guard on fact (note) and prose (text, cite).

prop: Decision: the `verify` object gains `unverified`. It is present whenever at least one mint in the workspace is unverified, on every reply that carries a `verify` object, whatever that reply's status and verb, and absent otherwise. A mint is unverified when the most recently started of its recorded verifications ended `timeout`, `unavailable` or `unparsable`. `ok`, including an `ok` with an incomplete leg, and `gated` count as verified. `unverified` carries `count` (all such mints) and `mints` (at most ten of their ids, most recently started first). A withdrawn mint is not listed. "Most recently started" cannot be read off the log as it stands, because a record's position, `seq` and `at` all mark when its verification finished, and two verifications of one mint can finish out of start order. So the ordering is owed a start mark, and a named test in which a revision's verification finishes before the one it superseded. The set shrinks only when a new verification of the mint completes. That takes a revision with changed text or citations, because an unchanged one starts nothing.

(1) `block` given a planted `timeout` record whose `detail` is "provider did not answer within the remaining budget" returns that string as `detail`. Red if the new insert is removed, since at the pinned commit `block` reads no record's detail.
(2) The same with an `ok` record whose `refuter_status` is set and whose `detail` is present: the detail is delivered beside `findings`. Red if the insert is guarded to non-`ok` statuses.

The sentinel is absent from the serialized `verify` object and present in the written record's log-only field. Red, per site, if that site's excerpt is formatted back into `detail`. (5) `unverified` over a planted log: mint A with a `timeout` started first and an `ok` started second, so A counts as verified; B `unavailable`; D `unparsable`; a withdrawn claim E `timeout`; and G, whose later-started verification (`ok`) is appended before its earlier-started one (`timeout`), which must still count as verified. Expected: `count` 2, `mints` [D, B] in start order, most recent first. The G row is red if ordering falls back to log position or `seq`, which is the out-of-order case in F9.

prop: Rejected alternatives. (a) A key outside the `verify` object, at the top level of the reply. Rejected so that "found nothing" (`ok`, no findings) and "did not look" (`timeout`, `unavailable`, `unparsable`) are read from one object and cannot be taken apart. (b) Surfacing unverified mints in `check`, `brief` or the rendered memo. Rejected because the module header keeps the verifier out of `check` and out of both report partitions, and its reason applies: a non-repeating model call there "would make a scope string promise coverage `check` does not have". (c) An automatic retry, or a circuit breaker that stops dispatching after repeated failures. Either changes what the verifier does, not what it says, and this design is scoped to the reply surface. (d) A rolling failure rate instead of a set of mints. A rate names no mint to act on and never shrinks when the author fixes one. (e) Refusing a mint, or returning an error, when verification fails. The module header states that nothing in the verifier can fail a mint.

Deferred and residual. Deferred: a way to re-run a mint's failed verification without changing its text. Today an unchanged revision starts nothing (the guard in the claim, fact and prose handlers), so after this design the author is told that a mint is unchecked but can clear it only by changing its wording or citations. That is a behaviour change, and a follow-up ticket should be filed if the `unverified` list turns out to stay non-empty in practice. Residual 1: under `queued`, `skipped`, `off`, `gated` and `unauthorized`, `guidance` still carries the findings-shaped constant. Residual 2: keeping reply text out of `detail` is enforced per site by tests, not by the type. Residual 3: a mint minted while verification was off, or while `spawn` returned false, has no record and is never listed, because `unverified` counts only verifications that were attempted and lost. Residual 4: a mint whose revision is still being verified stays listed under its older failed record until the new record lands. Residual 5: `detail` from a transport failure carries ureq's error text, which may name the endpoint. At the pinned commit `post` puts the API key only in the Authorization header, and no detail string formats the key.

Decision (a change to make; at the pinned commit the `verify` object has no such key): the `verify` object will gain `unverified`. While `verify.enabled` is true, it will be present on every reply that carries a `verify` object whenever at least one mint in the workspace is unverified, and absent otherwise. It is present whatever that reply's status and verb, including a reply whose own verb is not verified (status `off`). A mint will count as unverified when the record of its highest-revision recorded verification ended `timeout`, `unavailable` or `unparsable`. `ok`, including an `ok` with an incomplete leg, and `gated` count as verified. A mint whose newer verification is still in flight keeps its older record's standing until the newer record lands. `unverified` will carry `count` (all such mints) and `mints` (at most ten ids, highest-revision failures first, then by log position). Withdrawn claims are excluded. Facts and prose blocks have no withdrawal. The ordering key is the subject's revision number, not the record's position, `seq` or `at`: those three all mark when a verification finished, and two verifications of one mint can finish out of order. `Subject` and `Record` will gain `revision`, the mint's `revisions` count after the call that dispatched it (0 for a create). The constructors set it from the ledger they already read, or from a value their caller passes. Unlike a clock value, the count is persisted per mint, only increases, and cannot tie within one mint. A record without it (written before the change) sorts behind every record of the same mint that has one, by log position. The tally is computed in `verify_block` from the records `peek_delivered` already parses on every call, handed back beside the delivered record, and passed into `block`. It therefore costs no second read of verify.log. claims.jsonl is read only when some failing mint is a claim. A record torn mid-append is skipped by the tolerant reader and counted on a later call. The set shrinks only when a new verification of the mint completes, which takes a revision with changed text or citations, because an unchanged one starts nothing.
why: Advisor's joint read. Key the ordering on the mint's `revisions` rather than wall-clock time (`now_unix` is whole seconds, and a clock key is fragile). Compute the tally from the log `peek_delivered` already parses, instead of a second read. Load claims only when a failing id is a claim. State that withdrawal is claims-only and that the key rides on replies whose own verb is off.

A mint whose newer verification is still in flight keeps its older record's standing until the newer record lands. `unverified` will carry `count` (all such mints) and `mints` (at most ten ids, highest-revision failures first, then by log position). Withdrawn claims are excluded. Facts and prose blocks have no withdrawal. The ordering key is the subject's revision number, not the record's position, `seq` or `at`: those three all mark when a verification finished, and two verifications of one mint can finish out of order. `Subject` and `Record` will gain `revision`, the mint's `revisions` count after the call that dispatched it (0 for a create). The constructors set it from the ledger they already read, or from a value their caller passes. Unlike a clock value, the count is persisted per mint, only increases, and cannot tie within one mint. A record without it (written before the change) sorts behind every record of the same mint that has one, by log position. The tally is computed in `verify_block` from the records `peek_delivered` already parses on every call, handed back beside the delivered record, and passed into `block`. prop: Decision (a change to make; at the pinned commit `block` sends GUIDANCE on every status, per F5): after the change, under `timeout`, `unavailable` and `unparsable`, `guidance` will be a second constant instead of GUIDANCE. why: Follow F22's correction: a reword discards digest-carrying grounding records, not every record.

prop: At the pinned commit, a verification that ends `timeout`, `unavailable` or `unparsable` reaches the author as a `status` value on the reply whose cursor position holds its record, since delivery is one record per call. prop: Decision (a change to make; at the pinned commit no delivered record's `detail` reaches the reply, per C2): after the change, a reply that delivers a `timeout`, `unavailable` or `unparsable` record will carry that record's `detail`. On those records the leg that failed is the last leg `run` executed, because only the classify and check legs can end a verification with a non-`ok` status, and each returns at once on its own failure. Under `ok` and `gated`, no record detail is delivered. There, `detail` is whatever leg last wrote it, possibly a retried draw that later succeeded, and the `*_incomplete` qualifiers already name which leg did not complete. `unauthorized` keeps today's behaviour: `detail` comes from `missing`, computed from the current settings, because the `Unauthorized` returns inside `run` write no detail of their own. Model or provider reply text is excluded: it will stay in verify.log and never be sent to the author. At the pinned commit, four of the 20 detail sources embed such text: the 200-character reply beginnings in the check leg, the typed call and the literal check, and the label string in parse_assertions. The other sixteen are built from fixed strings, HTTP status codes, ureq transport errors (two sites), byte counts, budgets, draw numbers and token caps, part or question indices, and configuration. Keeping reply text out follows the rule the module already applies to a model-produced span that fails verification: a fabricated span sends the reader to check against text that does not exist.
why: Grounder: the categories for the sixteen omitted draw numbers, token caps and part indices, and ureq error text comes from two sites.

prop: Decision (a change to make, not a description of the pinned code): the implementation will split reply text off at its four sources rather than cut it out of the finished string later. At the pinned commit three of those sites (the check leg, the typed call and the literal check) format a 200-character excerpt straight into `detail`. The fourth, parse_assertions, formats the label into the `Err` string it returns, and `run` stores that string as `detail`. So splitting that site changes what parse_assertions returns: it will return the explanation and the label separately. After the change, each site will record the explanation as `detail` and the model or provider text as a separate log-only field on the record. `block` will read only `detail`, and verify-report will print the log-only field only under `--spans`. The split also repairs the report. The report dedups details as whole strings and truncates each to 160 characters, so today a detail carrying one of the three per-reply excerpts is unique on every record and is printed mostly as excerpt. Once the text is split off, identical causes collapse to one line. The other detail sources contain no reply text at the pinned commit, but nothing stops a future site from formatting reply text into `detail` itself. So the guarantee is per-site, pinned by the tests below, and not structural.
why: Grounder: parse_assertions returns its label in an Err string that `run` stores, so splitting it changes that function's return; only three sites carry 200-character excerpts.
